specStatements.text: Students should understand that meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed while mitosis leads to identical cells being formed.
Sexual reproduction involves the joining (fusion) of male and female gametes: sperm and egg cells in animals; pollen and egg cells in flowering plants.
In sexual reproduction there is mixing of genetic information which leads to variety in the offspring. The formation of gametes involves meiosis.
Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes. There is no mixing of genetic information. This leads to genetically identical offspring (clones). Only mitosis is involved.
Students should be able to explain how meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes and fertilisation restores the full number of chromosomes.
Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes.

When a cell divides to form gametes: copies of the genetic information are made; the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes; all gametes are genetically different from each other.
Gametes join at fertilisation to restore the normal number of chromosomes. The new cell divides by mitosis. The number of cells increases. As the embryo develops cells differentiate.
Knowledge of the stages of meiosis is not required.

Advantages of sexual reproduction: produces variation in the offspring; if the environment changes variation gives a survival advantage by natural selection; natural selection can be speeded up by humans in selective breeding to increase food production.

Advantages of asexual reproduction: only one parent needed; more time and energy efficient as do not need to find a mate; faster than sexual reproduction; many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.

Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances. Malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host, but sexually in the mosquito.; Many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but also reproduce sexually to give variation.; Many plants produce seeds sexually, but also reproduce asexually by runners such as strawberry plants, or bulb division such as daffodils.
Knowledge of reproduction in organisms is restricted to those mentioned.
Students are expected to be able to explain the advantages and disadvantages of asexual and sexual reproduction for any organism if given appropriate information.
Students should be able to describe the structure of DNA and define genome.

The genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed of a chemical called DNA. DNA is a polymer made up of two strands forming a double helix. The DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes.
A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
The genome of an organism is the entire genetic material of that organism. The whole human genome has now been studied and this will have great importance for medicine in the future.
Students should be able to discuss the importance of understanding the human genome.
This is limited to the: search for genes linked to different types of disease; understanding and treatment of inherited disorders; use in tracing human migration patterns from the past.

Students should be able to describe DNA as a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar.
DNA contains four bases, A, C, G and T.
A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid. The order of bases controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a particular protein.
The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections. Attached to each sugar is one of the four bases.
The DNA polymer is made up of repeating nucleotide units.

Students should be able to: recall a simple description of protein synthesis; explain simply how the structure of DNA affects the protein made; describe how genetic variants may influence phenotype: a) in coding DNA by altering the activity of a protein: and b) in non-coding DNA by altering how genes are expressed.
In the complementary strands a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand and a T to an A.
Students are not expected to know or understand the structure of mRNA, tRNA, or the detailed structure of amino acids or proteins.
Students should be able to explain how a change in DNA structure may result in a change in the protein synthesised by a gene.
Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.
When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape. This unique shape enables the proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or forming structures in the body such as collagen.
Mutations occur continuously. Most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.
A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape. An enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site or a structural protein may lose its strength.
Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.
Students should be able to explain the terms: gamete; chromosome; gene; allele; dominant; recessive; homozygous; heterozygous; genotype; phenotype.
Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as: fur colour in mice; and red-green colour blindness in humans. Each gene may have different forms called alleles.
The alleles present, or genotype, operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that can be expressed as a phenotype.
A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present (therefore no dominant allele present).
If the two alleles present are the same the organism is homozygous for that trait, but if the alleles are different they are heterozygous.
Most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting, rather than a single gene.

Students should be able to understand the concept of probability in predicting the results of a single gene cross, but recall that most phenotype features are the result of multiple genes rather than single gene inheritance.
Students should be able to use direct proportion and simple ratios to express the outcome of a genetic cross.
Students should be able to complete a Punnett square diagram and extract and interpret information from genetic crosses and family trees.
Students should be able to construct a genetic cross by Punnett square diagram and use it to make predictions using the theory of probability.

Some disorders are inherited. These disorders are caused by the inheritance of certain alleles. Polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele.; Cystic fibrosis (a disorder of cell membranes) is caused by a recessive allele.
Students should make informed judgements about the economic, social and ethical issues concerning embryo screening, given appropriate information.
Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes.
22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex. In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX).; In males the chromosomes are different (XY).
Students should to be able to carry out a genetic cross to show sex inheritance.
Students should understand and use direct proportion and simple ratios in genetic crosses.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No content describes the stages of meiosis. Meiosis is treated only as a division in reproductive organs that copies the genetic information, divides twice to form four genetically different gametes each with a single set of chromosomes.

Examples of organisms reproducing by both methods are limited to those named in the specification: malarial parasites, fungi, strawberry plants (runners) and daffodils (bulb division). No other named organism is used for recall; other organisms appear only as stimulus information that students interpret.

Discussion of the importance of the human genome is limited to the three listed uses: the search for genes linked to different types of disease, the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders, and tracing human migration patterns from the past.

Protein synthesis is described only as taking place on ribosomes according to a template, with carrier molecules bringing specific amino acids. mRNA, tRNA, transcription, translation and the detailed structure of amino acids or proteins are not named or explained anywhere in this set.

concepts.definition: The type of cell division that leads to non-identical cells being formed. It takes place in the reproductive organs to form gametes, and all the gametes produced are genetically different from each other.

The type of cell division that leads to identical cells being formed. It is the only division involved in asexual reproduction, and it is the division by which the new cell formed at fertilisation increases the number of cells.
Reproduction involving the joining (fusion) of male and female gametes. Because there is mixing of genetic information from two parents, it leads to variety in the offspring.

A sex cell that joins with another gamete at fertilisation. In animals the gametes are sperm and egg cells; in flowering plants they are pollen and egg cells. A gamete contains a single set of chromosomes.
Reproduction involving only one parent and no fusion of gametes. There is no mixing of genetic information, only mitosis is involved, and the offspring are genetically identical to the parent.
An offspring that is genetically identical to its parent. Clones are produced by asexual reproduction because only mitosis is involved and there is no mixing of genetic information.

Cells in the reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes. Copies of the genetic information are made, then the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes and all genetically different from each other.
The joining of two gametes, which restores the normal number of chromosomes. Meiosis halves the chromosome number in the gametes, so fertilisation of two gametes brings the full number back.
After fertilisation the new cell divides by mitosis so the number of cells increases. As the embryo develops these cells differentiate, becoming specialised for different jobs.

Sexual reproduction produces variation in the offspring. If the environment changes, variation gives a survival advantage by natural selection. Natural selection can also be speeded up by humans in selective breeding to increase food production.

Asexual reproduction needs only one parent, so it is more time and energy efficient as there is no need to find a mate. It is faster than sexual reproduction and many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.

Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances. Malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host but sexually in the mosquito; many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but also sexually to give variation; many plants produce seeds sexually but also reproduce asexually by runners, such as strawberry plants, or bulb division, such as daffodils.
The chemical of which the genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed. DNA is a polymer made up of two strands forming a double helix, and it is contained in structures called chromosomes.
A structure in the nucleus that contains the DNA. Genes are carried as small sections of DNA along a chromosome.
A small section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
The entire genetic material of an organism. The whole human genome has now been studied and this will have great importance for medicine in the future.

concepts.term: Importance of understanding the human genome
concepts.definition: Understanding the human genome matters for three reasons: the search for genes linked to different types of disease, the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders, and its use in tracing human migration patterns from the past.

The repeating unit from which the DNA polymer is made. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar, and DNA is made from four different nucleotides.
DNA contains four bases, A, C, G and T. One of these bases is attached to the sugar of each nucleotide, and the order of the bases carries the code.
A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid. The order of bases therefore controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a particular protein.
The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections. Attached to each sugar is one of the four bases.
In the complementary strands of the double helix a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand, and a T to an A.
Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.
When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape. This unique shape enables proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or forming structures in the body such as collagen.
A change in DNA structure. Mutations occur continuously, and most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.

concepts.term: Effect of a mutation on a protein
concepts.definition: A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape. An enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site, or a structural protein may lose its strength.
Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.
One of the different forms a gene may have. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans.
An allele that is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present, and therefore no dominant allele is present.
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are the same.
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are different.
The alleles present in an organism. The genotype operates at a molecular level to develop characteristics.
The characteristics that the genotype develops and that are expressed in the organism.
Most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting, rather than a single gene, so most phenotype features are not the result of single gene inheritance.

A diagram used to set out a genetic cross by combining the alleles carried by the gametes of each parent. The outcome can be expressed using direct proportion or simple ratios, and gives the probability of each genotype rather than a guaranteed result.

Disorders caused by the inheritance of certain alleles. Polydactyly, having extra fingers or toes, is caused by a dominant allele. Cystic fibrosis, a disorder of cell membranes, is caused by a recessive allele.

Screening embryos for the alleles that cause inherited disorders. It raises economic, social and ethical issues about which students should make informed judgements when given appropriate information.

Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes. 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex: in females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX) and in males they are different (XY).

misconceptions.question: Are the cells produced by meiosis identical to each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed; all the gametes produced are genetically different from each other. It is mitosis that leads to identical cells being formed.
misconceptions.misconception: Meiosis produces genetically identical cells, in the same way that mitosis does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both meiosis and mitosis are taught as 'cell division' and both start by making copies of the genetic information, so students merge them into one process and carry the identical-cell outcome of mitosis across to meiosis.
misconceptions.correction: Meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed while mitosis leads to identical cells being formed. In sexual reproduction the mixing of genetic information leads to variety in the offspring.

misconceptions.question: Does asexual reproduction involve gametes joining?
misconceptions.correct: No. Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes, so there is no mixing of genetic information.
misconceptions.misconception: Asexual reproduction involves the fusion of gametes, just with one parent supplying both of them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that reproduction means making a new organism and associate all reproduction with gametes, so they assume the gametes must still fuse even when only one parent is involved.
misconceptions.correction: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes. There is no mixing of genetic information and only mitosis is involved, which leads to genetically identical offspring (clones).

misconceptions.question: How many gametes are formed when one cell divides by meiosis?
misconceptions.correct: Four. The cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes.
misconceptions.misconception: Meiosis produces two gametes from one cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that meiosis halves the chromosome number and wrongly apply the same halving to the number of cells, or they recall mitosis producing two cells and assume meiosis does the same.
misconceptions.correction: When a cell divides to form gametes, copies of the genetic information are made and the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes and all genetically different from each other.

misconceptions.question: How many sets of chromosomes does a gamete contain?
misconceptions.correct: One. Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes, so each gamete has a single set of chromosomes.
misconceptions.misconception: A gamete contains the full number of chromosomes, the same as an ordinary body cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that copies of the genetic information are made at the start of the division, so they assume every cell produced ends up with a complete set.
misconceptions.correction: Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes: the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes. Fertilisation then restores the full number of chromosomes.

misconceptions.question: Which type of cell division makes the embryo grow after fertilisation?
misconceptions.correct: Mitosis. The new cell formed at fertilisation divides by mitosis, so the number of cells increases and, as the embryo develops, cells differentiate.
misconceptions.misconception: The new cell formed at fertilisation divides by meiosis to produce the embryo.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Meiosis has just been met in the context of reproduction, so students attach it to every stage of reproduction rather than only to the formation of gametes.
misconceptions.correction: Gametes join at fertilisation to restore the normal number of chromosomes. The new cell then divides by mitosis, the number of cells increases, and as the embryo develops cells differentiate.

misconceptions.question: Which is faster and more energy efficient, sexual or asexual reproduction?
misconceptions.correct: Asexual reproduction. It needs only one parent, so it is more time and energy efficient as there is no need to find a mate, and it is faster than sexual reproduction.
misconceptions.misconception: Sexual reproduction is faster and needs less energy because two parents share the work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume that two parents means the effort is halved, and they treat sexual reproduction as the 'normal' and therefore most efficient method because it is the one they know best.
misconceptions.correction: Advantages of asexual reproduction are that only one parent is needed, it is more time and energy efficient as there is no need to find a mate, it is faster than sexual reproduction, and many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.

misconceptions.question: Does asexual reproduction produce variation in the offspring?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is no mixing of genetic information in asexual reproduction, so the offspring are genetically identical clones.
misconceptions.misconception: Asexual reproduction produces variation in the offspring, just less of it than sexual reproduction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see variation between individual plants or fungi grown from the same parent and assume the differences must be genetic, rather than caused by the environment.
misconceptions.correction: Asexual reproduction involves no fusion of gametes and no mixing of genetic information, which leads to genetically identical offspring (clones). It is sexual reproduction that produces variation in the offspring.

misconceptions.question: Can one species reproduce both sexually and asexually?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances, such as malarial parasites, many fungi and many plants.
misconceptions.misconception: Each species reproduces by one method only, either sexually or asexually.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sexual and asexual reproduction are taught as a pair of opposites and compared in tables, so students treat them as two exclusive categories that organisms are sorted into.
misconceptions.correction: Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances: malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host but sexually in the mosquito; many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but also sexually to give variation; many plants produce seeds sexually but also reproduce asexually by runners or bulb division.

misconceptions.question: Is a gene the same thing as a chromosome?
misconceptions.correct: No. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome, so a chromosome carries many genes.
misconceptions.misconception: A gene and a chromosome are the same structure under two different names.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words gene, chromosome and DNA are used in the same sentences and diagrams without a clear sense of scale, so students treat them as interchangeable labels.
misconceptions.correction: The DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes, and a gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids.

misconceptions.question: What does the genome of an organism include?
misconceptions.correct: The entire genetic material of that organism, not only the parts that code for proteins.
misconceptions.misconception: The genome is just the collection of genes that code for proteins.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word genome sounds like a plural of gene, so students read it as 'all the genes' and leave out the rest of the genetic material.
misconceptions.correction: The genome of an organism is the entire genetic material of that organism. Not all parts of DNA code for proteins.

misconceptions.question: What is DNA made up of?
misconceptions.correct: DNA is a polymer made up of repeating nucleotide units, each with a common sugar and phosphate group and one of four bases.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA is made up of a chain of amino acids.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that DNA codes for a sequence of amino acids and that both DNA and protein are polymers, so they attach the amino acid unit to the wrong molecule.
misconceptions.correction: DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar. It is the protein, not the DNA, that is a sequence of amino acids.

misconceptions.question: What does a gene code for?
misconceptions.correct: A particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
misconceptions.misconception: A gene codes directly for a characteristic, such as eye colour or height.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday phrases like 'the gene for blue eyes' skip the protein step entirely, so students learn a direct gene-to-characteristic link.
misconceptions.correction: A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome, and each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein. The alleles present operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that can be expressed as a phenotype.

misconceptions.question: How many bases code for one amino acid?
misconceptions.correct: Three. A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid.
misconceptions.misconception: One base codes for one amino acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the four bases lined up along the strand and match them one-to-one with the units of the protein, because a one-to-one code seems simpler.
misconceptions.correction: A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid, and the order of bases controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a particular protein.

misconceptions.question: What forms the long strands of a DNA molecule?
misconceptions.correct: Alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with one of the four bases attached to each sugar.
misconceptions.misconception: The four bases join end to end to form the two long strands of DNA.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams draw attention to the lettered bases in the middle of the molecule, and students read the sequence of letters as though it were the strand itself.
misconceptions.correction: The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections. Attached to each sugar is one of the four bases.

misconceptions.question: Which bases pair together in the complementary strands?
misconceptions.correct: A C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand, and a T to an A.
misconceptions.misconception: In the complementary strands A pairs with C and G pairs with T.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember only that the bases pair up and recall the list 'A, C, G, T' in order, pairing the first with the second and the third with the fourth.
misconceptions.correction: In the complementary strands a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand and a T to an A.

misconceptions.question: Where in the cell are proteins synthesised?
misconceptions.correct: On ribosomes, according to a template.
misconceptions.misconception: Proteins are synthesised in the nucleus, where the DNA is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the genetic material is in the nucleus and assume the protein must be built in the same place as the instructions are stored.
misconceptions.correction: Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.

misconceptions.question: Does every mutation change the protein that is produced?
misconceptions.correct: No. Mutations occur continuously, and most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.
misconceptions.misconception: Every mutation alters the protein and therefore changes the organism.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mutations are met mainly through examples of inherited disorders, so students only ever see the rare mutations that do have an effect.
misconceptions.correction: Mutations occur continuously. Most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed. A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape.

misconceptions.question: Can DNA that does not code for a protein affect the phenotype?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas may affect how genes are expressed.
misconceptions.misconception: Non-coding DNA has no effect on the phenotype because it does not code for a protein.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The label 'non-coding' sounds like 'does nothing', and students have been taught that characteristics come from proteins, so DNA that makes no protein seems irrelevant.
misconceptions.correction: Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.

misconceptions.question: What allows a protein to do its job?
misconceptions.correct: Its unique shape. When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape that enables it to work as an enzyme, hormone or structure such as collagen.
misconceptions.misconception: A protein's job is decided by how many amino acids it contains, not by its folded shape.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students focus on the order of bases coding for a chain of amino acids and stop at the chain, never picturing the folding step that follows.
misconceptions.correction: When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape. This unique shape enables the proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or forming structures in the body such as collagen.

misconceptions.question: Does a dominant allele have to be the most common allele in a population?
misconceptions.correct: No. Dominant means the allele is always expressed even if only one copy is present; it says nothing about how common it is.
misconceptions.misconception: A dominant allele is the allele that most of the population carries.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of 'dominant' is 'most widespread' or 'strongest', and students transfer that meaning to the genetic term.
misconceptions.correction: A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present.

misconceptions.question: How many copies of a recessive allele are needed for it to be expressed?
misconceptions.correct: Two. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present, so no dominant allele is present.
misconceptions.misconception: A recessive allele is expressed whenever it is present, even as a single copy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that if an allele is in the genotype it must show up in the phenotype, because they think of the genotype as a list of visible features.
misconceptions.correction: A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present (therefore no dominant allele present).

misconceptions.question: Are the genotype and the phenotype the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. The genotype is the alleles present; the phenotype is the characteristic that those alleles develop.
misconceptions.misconception: The genotype and the phenotype are two words for the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two terms are introduced together, sound alike, and are often written side by side in the same table row, so students do not separate the alleles from the characteristic they produce.
misconceptions.correction: The alleles present, or genotype, operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics that can be expressed as a phenotype.

misconceptions.question: What does heterozygous mean?
misconceptions.correct: That the two alleles present for that trait are different.
misconceptions.misconception: Heterozygous means having two copies of the same allele.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two long words homozygous and heterozygous look similar and are learned as a pair, so students match the definitions to the wrong terms.
misconceptions.correction: If the two alleles present are the same the organism is homozygous for that trait, but if the alleles are different they are heterozygous.

misconceptions.question: Is every characteristic controlled by a single gene?
misconceptions.correct: No. Most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting, rather than a single gene.
misconceptions.misconception: Every characteristic is controlled by one single gene.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Genetic crosses and Punnett squares are always taught using single gene examples such as fur colour in mice, so students generalise that pattern to all characteristics.
misconceptions.correction: Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans, but most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting.

misconceptions.question: If a cross predicts a 3:1 ratio, will exactly three of every four offspring show the characteristic?
misconceptions.correct: No. The ratio gives the probability of each outcome; the actual offspring produced may be in different proportions.
misconceptions.misconception: A predicted 3:1 ratio means exactly three out of every four offspring will show the characteristic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A Punnett square has exactly four boxes, so students read the four boxes as four actual offspring rather than as four equally likely outcomes.
misconceptions.correction: A Punnett square diagram is used to make predictions using the theory of probability. The outcome of a genetic cross is expressed using direct proportion and simple ratios as a prediction, not as a guaranteed count of offspring.

misconceptions.question: Which allele causes polydactyly and which causes cystic fibrosis?
misconceptions.correct: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele and cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele.
misconceptions.misconception: Polydactyly is caused by a recessive allele and cystic fibrosis by a dominant allele.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume that a serious disorder must be caused by a 'stronger' dominant allele and that a rarer, less harmful condition must be recessive, so they swap the two.
misconceptions.correction: Polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele. Cystic fibrosis (a disorder of cell membranes) is caused by a recessive allele.

misconceptions.question: Which parent's gamete determines the sex of a child?
misconceptions.correct: The father's. The mother's egg cells all carry an X chromosome, while sperm cells carry either an X or a Y.
misconceptions.misconception: The mother's egg cell determines the sex of the child.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pregnancy is associated entirely with the mother, so students assume she must control every feature of the developing embryo, including its sex.
misconceptions.correction: In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX) and in males they are different (XY). A genetic cross between XX and XY shows that the gamete carrying either an X or a Y determines the sex of the offspring.

misconceptions.question: How many chromosomes are in an ordinary human body cell?
misconceptions.correct: 46, arranged as 23 pairs.
misconceptions.misconception: An ordinary human body cell contains 23 chromosomes in total.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number 23 is the one students remember from the phrase '23 pairs', and they drop the word 'pairs' when recalling it.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes. 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex.

misconceptions.question: Which division do cells in the reproductive organs use to form gametes?
misconceptions.correct: Meiosis. Cells in the reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes.
misconceptions.misconception: Gametes are formed by mitosis in the reproductive organs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mitosis is the division students meet first and use for all growth and repair, so they apply it as the default division for making any new cell.
misconceptions.correction: Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes, and all gametes are genetically different from each other.

misconceptions.question: Where in a cell is the genetic material found?
misconceptions.correct: In the nucleus. The genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed of DNA, contained in structures called chromosomes.
misconceptions.misconception: The genetic material is stored loose in the cytoplasm of the cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the cell as a bag of contents and remember that ribosomes and other structures are in the cytoplasm, so they place the DNA there too.
misconceptions.correction: The genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed of a chemical called DNA. The DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes.

misconceptions.question: What kinds of issues does embryo screening raise?
misconceptions.correct: Economic, social and ethical issues, about which informed judgements should be made.
misconceptions.misconception: Embryo screening raises only medical issues, because it is a medical procedure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Screening is presented in a health context, so students judge it purely by whether it works, without considering its cost, its effect on society or the ethical questions it raises.
misconceptions.correction: Students should make informed judgements about the economic, social and ethical issues concerning embryo screening, given appropriate information.

misconceptions.question: Which sex chromosomes are found in females and which in males?
misconceptions.correct: In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX); in males they are different (XY).
misconceptions.misconception: In females the sex chromosomes are XY and in males they are XX.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember only that one sex has two different chromosomes but not which, and the letters are easy to swap when they are recalled without the XX and XY labels attached.
misconceptions.correction: 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex. In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX); in males the chromosomes are different (XY).

misconceptions.question: Which process halves the number of chromosomes?
misconceptions.correct: Meiosis. Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes, and fertilisation then restores the full number.
misconceptions.misconception: It is fertilisation that halves the number of chromosomes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two processes are always described in the same sentence, and 'fertilisation' is the more memorable word, so students attach the halving to the wrong one.
misconceptions.correction: Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes and fertilisation restores the full number of chromosomes.

misconceptions.question: Is a base the same thing as a nucleotide?
misconceptions.correct: No. A nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar.
misconceptions.misconception: The four different nucleotides are simply the four bases A, C, G and T.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students only ever write out DNA as a string of letters, so the base is the only part of the unit they ever see named, and the word nucleotide becomes another name for it.
misconceptions.correction: DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the cells formed by meiosis?

options.text: They are all genetically identical to each other.
options.rationale: A student who thinks meiosis works like mitosis expects identical cells. It is mitosis that leads to identical cells being formed; meiosis leads to non-identical cells.

options.text: They are all genetically different from each other.
options.rationale: Meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed: all gametes are genetically different from each other.

options.text: There are two of them formed from the parent cell.
options.rationale: A student who transfers the halving of chromosome number to the number of cells expects two. The cell divides twice to form four gametes.

options.text: They each contain the full number of chromosomes.
options.rationale: A student who remembers that copies of the genetic information are made expects full sets. Each gamete has a single set of chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about sexual reproduction in a flowering plant is correct?

options.text: In plants, the gametes made by meiosis are all identical cells.
options.rationale: A student who merges meiosis with mitosis expects identical products. Meiosis leads to non-identical cells, which is why there is variety in the offspring.

options.text: In plants, pollen and egg cells fuse, mixing genetic information.
options.rationale: Sexual reproduction involves the joining (fusion) of male and female gametes, which in flowering plants are pollen and egg cells, and there is mixing of genetic information.

options.text: In plants, one parent's gametes fuse without a second parent.
options.rationale: A student who thinks any reproduction must involve fusing gametes applies fusion to a single parent. Sexual reproduction is the fusion of male and female gametes; one-parent reproduction involves no fusion of gametes.

options.text: In plants, the gametes are made by mitosis in flower organs.
options.rationale: A student who treats mitosis as the default division expects it to make gametes. Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes asexual reproduction?

options.text: One parent is involved and meiosis forms identical cells.
options.rationale: A student who thinks meiosis produces identical cells uses it to explain cloning. Only mitosis is involved in asexual reproduction, and meiosis forms non-identical cells.

options.text: One parent is involved and its gametes fuse together.
options.rationale: A student who links all reproduction with gametes keeps the fusion step. Asexual reproduction involves no fusion of gametes.

options.text: One parent is involved and the offspring show variation.
options.rationale: A student who sees differences between offspring assumes they are genetic. There is no mixing of genetic information, so the offspring are genetically identical.

options.text: One parent is involved and only mitosis takes place.
options.rationale: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent, no fusion of gametes, and only mitosis, so the offspring are genetically identical clones.

mcqs.stem: A cell in the reproductive organ of a mouse divides to form gametes. What is the result?

options.text: Two cells form by meiosis, both genetically different.
options.rationale: A student who recalls one division, as in mitosis, expects two cells. The cell divides twice to form four gametes.

options.text: Four cells form by mitosis, all genetically identical.
options.rationale: A student who treats mitosis as the division that makes new cells applies it here. Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes.

options.text: Four cells form by meiosis, all genetically different.
options.rationale: Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis; the cell divides twice to form four gametes, all genetically different from each other.

options.text: Four cells form by meiosis, all genetically identical now.
options.rationale: A student who thinks meiosis gives identical cells keeps the number right but the outcome wrong. All gametes are genetically different from each other.

mcqs.stem: A body cell of a species contains 20 chromosomes. What happens to chromosome number during reproduction?

options.text: Meiosis gives gametes with 20; fertilisation reduces to 10.
options.rationale: A student who attaches the halving to fertilisation reverses the two processes. Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes and fertilisation restores the full number.

options.text: Meiosis gives gametes with 10; fertilisation restores 20.
options.rationale: Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes, so each gamete has a single set of 10, and fertilisation restores the full number of 20.

options.text: Meiosis gives two gametes with 10; fertilisation gives 20.
options.rationale: A student who expects one division to give two cells gets the chromosome numbers right but the gamete number wrong. The cell divides twice to form four gametes.

options.text: Meiosis gives gametes with 20; fertilisation restores 40.
options.rationale: A student who thinks gametes keep the full number doubles it at fertilisation. Each gamete has a single set of chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: What happens after two gametes join at fertilisation?

options.text: The new cell divides by meiosis, then cells differentiate.
options.rationale: A student who links meiosis to everything in reproduction uses it for growth too. The new cell formed at fertilisation divides by mitosis.

options.text: The new cell divides by mitosis and then forms four gametes.
options.rationale: A student who thinks mitosis makes gametes expects gametes as the product. Gametes are made by meiosis in the reproductive organs, before fertilisation.

options.text: The new cell divides by mitosis and cells differentiate.
options.rationale: Gametes join at fertilisation to restore the normal number of chromosomes; the new cell divides by mitosis, the number of cells increases, and as the embryo develops cells differentiate.

options.text: The new cell has half the chromosome number of gametes.
options.rationale: A student who thinks fertilisation halves chromosome number applies it to the new cell. Fertilisation restores the normal number of chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: A grower has one healthy strawberry plant and wants many identical plants quickly. Why is reproduction by runners an advantage here?

options.text: Two parents share the work, so less time and energy are needed here.
options.rationale: A student who thinks two parents halve the effort picks this. Asexual reproduction is more time and energy efficient because there is no need to find a mate.

options.text: One parent is needed and it is faster than sexual reproduction.
options.rationale: Advantages of asexual reproduction are that only one parent is needed, it is faster than sexual reproduction, and many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.

options.text: The offspring produced will show useful variation from the parent.
options.rationale: A student who thinks asexual reproduction gives variation picks this. There is no mixing of genetic information, so the offspring are genetically identical clones.

options.text: The plant can use only one method, so it cannot produce any seeds.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a species uses one method only rules out seeds. Many plants produce seeds sexually but also reproduce asexually by runners.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about organisms that reproduce by both methods is correct?

options.text: Daffodils reproduce by bulb division, fusing gametes.
options.rationale: A student who thinks all reproduction involves fusion adds it to bulb division. Bulb division is asexual reproduction, with no fusion of gametes.

options.text: Malarial parasites reproduce only by one method, asexually.
options.rationale: A student who sorts each species into one method picks this. Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances.

options.text: Fungi reproduce asexually by spores to give variation.
options.rationale: A student who thinks asexual reproduction gives variation links the spores to variation. Many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but reproduce sexually to give variation.

options.text: Malarial parasites reproduce sexually in the mosquito.
options.rationale: Malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host, but sexually in the mosquito.

mcqs.stem: A population of fungi lives in a habitat where conditions are beginning to change. Why may reproducing sexually be an advantage?

options.text: Asexual reproduction is what produces the variation needed in this habitat.
options.rationale: A student who thinks asexual reproduction gives variation picks the wrong method. There is no mixing of genetic information in asexual reproduction.

options.text: It is faster and uses less energy than reproducing asexually would be.
options.rationale: A student who thinks two parents are more efficient picks speed. Asexual reproduction is the faster and more energy efficient method.

options.text: It produces variation, giving a survival advantage by natural selection.
options.rationale: Sexual reproduction produces variation in the offspring, and if the environment changes variation gives a survival advantage by natural selection.

options.text: Fungi can use only one method, so they have to reproduce sexually here.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a species uses one method only reasons this way. Many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but also reproduce sexually.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the structure of DNA?

options.text: A chemical stored loosely in the cell's cytoplasm
options.rationale: A student who pictures the cell contents mixed together places DNA outside the nucleus. The genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed of DNA.

options.text: A polymer of four bases joined into two long strands
options.rationale: A student who reads the lettered bases as the strand itself picks this. The long strands consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with a base attached to each sugar.

options.text: A polymer of amino acids joined in one long chain
options.rationale: A student who knows DNA codes for amino acids makes DNA out of them. DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides; the protein is the chain of amino acids.

options.text: A polymer of two strands forming a double helix
options.rationale: DNA is a polymer made up of two strands forming a double helix, contained in structures called chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the genome of an organism?

options.text: The amino acids that make up an organism's DNA
options.rationale: A student who thinks DNA is built from amino acids describes the genome that way. DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides.

options.text: The parts of the DNA that code for proteins
options.rationale: A student who reads genome as 'all the genes' leaves out the rest. Not all parts of DNA code for proteins, and the genome is the entire genetic material.

options.text: The genetic material found in the cytoplasm
options.rationale: A student who places DNA in the cytoplasm defines the genome by the wrong location. The genetic material is in the nucleus of the cell.

options.text: The entire genetic material of an organism
options.rationale: The genome of an organism is the entire genetic material of that organism.

mcqs.stem: A gene in a mouse is linked to brown fur. What does that gene code for?

options.text: The brown fur characteristic directly
options.rationale: A student used to phrases like 'the gene for brown fur' skips the protein step. A gene codes for a sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein, and the alleles present operate at a molecular level to develop characteristics.

options.text: A certain sequence of amino acids
options.rationale: Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.

options.text: One amino acid for each single base
options.rationale: A student who matches bases to amino acids one to one picks this. A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid.

options.text: An entire chromosome in the nucleus
options.rationale: A student who treats gene and chromosome as the same structure picks this. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is one of the uses of understanding the human genome?

options.text: Finding the gene that directly builds a feature
options.rationale: A student who thinks a gene codes straight for a characteristic expects this use. Each gene codes for a sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.

options.text: Removing non-coding DNA, which has no effect
options.rationale: A student who thinks non-coding DNA does nothing sees it as removable. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off.

options.text: Searching for genes linked to some diseases
options.rationale: Understanding the human genome is important for the search for genes linked to different types of disease, the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders, and tracing human migration patterns from the past.

options.text: Listing all genes that code for a protein
options.rationale: A student who thinks the genome is only the coding genes describes it as a gene list. The genome is the entire genetic material, and this is not one of the listed uses.

mcqs.stem: DNA is a polymer. Which describes the repeating unit it is made from?

options.text: An amino acid joined to a sugar and phosphate group
options.rationale: A student who thinks DNA is built from amino acids puts one in the unit. The unit is a nucleotide, and amino acids are assembled into proteins.

options.text: A base joined directly on to the next base in the strand
options.rationale: A student who thinks the bases form the strands joins them to each other. The long strands consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections.

options.text: Just one of the four different bases, A, C, G or T
options.rationale: A student who treats base and nucleotide as the same thing picks a bare base. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one base attached to the sugar.

options.text: A nucleotide of sugar, phosphate and one of four bases
options.rationale: DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides; each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar.

mcqs.stem: A coding section of DNA contains 30 bases. How many amino acids does this code for?

options.text: 10, because three bases code for one amino acid
options.rationale: A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid, so 30 bases code for 10 amino acids.

options.text: 30, because one base codes for one amino acid
options.rationale: A student who matches each base to an amino acid divides by nothing. A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid.

options.text: 15, because each pair of bases codes for one acid
options.rationale: A student focused on bases pairing up uses two bases per amino acid. The code is a sequence of three bases for a particular amino acid.

options.text: 1, because the section codes for a characteristic
options.rationale: A student who thinks a gene codes for a characteristic sees one outcome. The order of bases controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a protein.

mcqs.stem: What forms the two long strands of a DNA molecule?

options.text: Nucleotides made only of the four bases
options.rationale: A student who treats a base as a whole nucleotide leaves out the backbone. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one base attached.

options.text: Alternating sugar and phosphate sections
options.rationale: The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with one of the four bases attached to each sugar.

options.text: Four bases joined end to end in order
options.rationale: A student who reads the base sequence as the strand picks this. The bases are attached to the sugars of the sugar and phosphate strand.

options.text: Amino acids joined end to end in chains
options.rationale: A student who thinks DNA is made of amino acids builds the strand from them. DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides.

mcqs.stem: In the complementary strands of DNA, how are the bases linked?

options.text: A is linked to C, while G is linked to T
options.rationale: A student who recalls the list A, C, G, T and pairs it in order picks this. A C is linked to a G and a T to an A.

options.text: Every base links to the next base along
options.rationale: A student who thinks the bases form the strand links them along it rather than across. The linking described is between the two complementary strands.

options.text: Each base links to a matching identical base
options.rationale: A student who treats bases as identical repeating units expects like to pair with like. A C is linked to a G, and a T to an A.

options.text: C is linked to G, and T is linked to A
options.rationale: In the complementary strands a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand and a T to an A.

mcqs.stem: Where are proteins synthesised, and how do the amino acids reach the chain?

options.text: On ribosomes; carrier molecules bring the amino acids
options.rationale: Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template, and carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.

options.text: On ribosomes; the DNA strand itself is the amino acids
options.rationale: A student who thinks DNA is made of amino acids has no need for carriers. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to the growing chain.

options.text: In the cytoplasm's DNA; carrier molecules bring bases
options.rationale: A student who places the DNA in the cytoplasm builds the protein there. The genetic material is in the nucleus, and proteins are synthesised on ribosomes.

options.text: In the nucleus; carrier molecules bring the amino acids
options.rationale: A student who thinks the protein is built where the DNA is kept picks the nucleus. Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template.

mcqs.stem: An enzyme is able to do its job because of which feature of the protein?

options.text: The characteristic that its gene codes for
options.rationale: A student who thinks genes code for characteristics explains the enzyme that way. A gene codes for a sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.

options.text: The number of amino acids in its finished chain
options.rationale: A student who stops at the chain judges the protein by its length. It is the unique shape formed when the chain folds that enables the protein to work.

options.text: The place in the nucleus where it was made
options.rationale: A student who thinks proteins are made in the nucleus looks there for the explanation. Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, and it is the folded shape that matters.

options.text: The unique shape it folds into at the end
options.rationale: When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape, and this unique shape enables proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or structures such as collagen.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about mutations is correct?

options.text: Each one alters the protein that is made.
options.rationale: A student who has only met harmful examples expects every mutation to have an effect. Most mutations do not alter the protein.

options.text: Most do not alter the protein produced.
options.rationale: Mutations occur continuously, and most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.

options.text: Only those in non-coding DNA have no effect.
options.rationale: A student who thinks non-coding DNA does nothing draws the line there. Variations in non-coding DNA may affect how genes are expressed, and most mutations anywhere do not alter the protein.

options.text: Each one alters a characteristic directly.
options.rationale: A student who links genes straight to characteristics expects a visible change. Mutations act on the protein made, and most do not alter it.

mcqs.stem: A mutation changes the shape of an enzyme. What is the likely effect?

options.text: The enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site.
options.rationale: A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape: an enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site, or a structural protein may lose its strength.

options.text: Every other protein in the cell is altered in the same way.
options.rationale: A student who thinks each mutation changes everything spreads the effect. A mutation affects the protein synthesised by that gene.

options.text: There is no effect, because this DNA is non-coding DNA.
options.rationale: A student who assumes non-coding DNA is inactive rules out any change. Here the mutation has altered a protein, and non-coding variations can still affect how genes are expressed.

options.text: The enzyme still works, because only its length matters.
options.rationale: A student who judges a protein by chain length sees no problem. The unique shape the protein folds into is what enables it to do its job.

mcqs.stem: A genetic variant is found in a non-coding part of DNA. How may it influence the phenotype?

options.text: By altering how genes are switched on and off
options.rationale: Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.

options.text: It has no way of influencing the phenotype at all
options.rationale: A student who reads 'non-coding' as 'does nothing' rules out any effect. Variations in non-coding DNA may affect how genes are expressed.

options.text: By coding directly for a new characteristic
options.rationale: A student who links DNA straight to characteristics expects a direct code. Not all parts of DNA code for proteins, and this part codes for none.

options.text: By altering the shape of every protein made
options.rationale: A student who thinks every change alters proteins applies it here. This variation alters how genes are expressed rather than a protein's shape.

mcqs.stem: A mouse has two different alleles for fur colour. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is homozygous, because two alleles are present here.
options.rationale: A student who muddles the similar terms picks homozygous. An organism is homozygous only if the two alleles present are the same.

options.text: It is heterozygous, so the recessive allele is expressed.
options.rationale: A student who thinks one copy is enough for a recessive allele picks this. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present.

options.text: It is heterozygous, so the dominant allele is shown.
options.rationale: If the alleles are different the organism is heterozygous, and a dominant allele is always expressed even if only one copy is present.

options.text: It is heterozygous, so genotype equals phenotype.
options.rationale: A student who merges the two terms treats them as one. The genotype is the alleles present, which operate to develop the phenotype.

mcqs.stem: A plant has the genotype Tt, where T is the dominant allele. What is its phenotype?

options.text: It shows T only if T is common in the population.
options.rationale: A student who reads dominant as 'most common' adds a condition. A dominant allele is always expressed even if only one copy is present.

options.text: It shows the characteristic of the t allele only.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a single copy of a recessive allele is expressed picks t. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present.

options.text: Its phenotype is written as the full genotype Tt.
options.rationale: A student who treats genotype and phenotype as the same writes the alleles. The phenotype is the characteristic that the alleles develop.

options.text: It shows the characteristic of the T allele.
options.rationale: A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present, so the alleles present develop the characteristic coded by T.

mcqs.stem: Two heterozygous mice (Bb) are crossed, where B is dominant. Which ratio of phenotypes does a Punnett square predict?

options.text: 3 with the dominant characteristic to 1 without
options.rationale: The Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb and bb. The dominant allele is expressed in the first three, so the predicted ratio is 3 to 1.

options.text: 1 with the dominant characteristic to 3 without
options.rationale: A student who thinks one copy of the recessive allele is expressed counts the three combinations containing b as showing the recessive characteristic. A recessive allele needs two copies.

options.text: 4 with the dominant characteristic to 0 without
options.rationale: A student who confuses homozygous and heterozygous treats both parents as BB, so every offspring carries B. Heterozygous parents each carry one B and one b.

options.text: 2 with the dominant characteristic and 2 without
options.rationale: A student who reads dominant as simply the commoner allele expects the two alleles to be shared out evenly. A dominant allele is expressed even with one copy, so three of the four combinations show it.

mcqs.stem: In a family tree, two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis have a child who does. What does this show?

options.text: The allele causing the disorder is dominant.
options.rationale: A student who swaps the two disorders calls this allele dominant. Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele; a dominant allele would be expressed in a parent.

options.text: The parents' genotype matches their phenotype.
options.rationale: A student who merges the two terms assumes an unaffected phenotype means no allele is carried. The genotype is the alleles present, which may include an unexpressed recessive allele.

options.text: Each parent carries one recessive allele.
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele, which is only expressed if two copies are present, so each unaffected parent must carry one copy to pass on.

options.text: Only one parent carries the recessive allele.
options.rationale: A student who thinks one copy is enough to be expressed needs only one carrier parent. Two copies are needed, so the child inherited one from each parent.

mcqs.stem: A student uses a single gene cross to predict a person's height. Why is this prediction unreliable?

options.text: Every characteristic is controlled by one single gene here.
options.rationale: A student who generalises from single gene examples sees no problem with the method. Most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting.

options.text: Most characteristics result from multiple genes interacting.
options.rationale: Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, but most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting rather than a single gene.

options.text: A gene codes directly for the characteristic, not protein.
options.rationale: A student who links genes straight to characteristics blames the coding step. Each gene codes for a sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.

options.text: A single cross gives exact numbers of offspring produced.
options.rationale: A student who reads the four boxes as four real offspring objects to the counting. A genetic cross gives probability, which is a separate point from multiple gene inheritance.

mcqs.stem: In mice, black fur (B) is dominant to brown (b). A black mouse is crossed with a brown mouse and some brown offspring are produced. What was the black parent's genotype?

options.text: BB, since its two alleles are the same
options.rationale: A student who confuses the terms assumes an organism showing a characteristic is homozygous. A BB parent could pass on only B, so no brown offspring could be produced.

options.text: bb, since a b allele was expressed here
options.rationale: A student who thinks a recessive allele is expressed with one copy reads brown offspring as proof of a bb parent. A bb mouse would itself be brown, not black.

options.text: Bb, since it passed on a b allele
options.rationale: A brown offspring must be bb, so it received a b allele from each parent. The black parent expressed B but also carried b, so its genotype was Bb.

options.text: BB, since B is the more common allele
options.rationale: A student who reads dominant as 'commonest' assumes two copies of B. Dominant describes expression with one copy, not frequency in the population.

mcqs.stem: Which alleles cause polydactyly and cystic fibrosis?

options.text: Polydactyly dominant; cystic fibrosis recessive
options.rationale: Polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele, and cystic fibrosis (a disorder of cell membranes) is caused by a recessive allele.

options.text: Both are dominant, as the disorders are common
options.rationale: A student who reads dominant as 'common' uses frequency to decide. Dominant means the allele is expressed even if only one copy is present.

options.text: Both are recessive, as one copy is enough here
options.rationale: A student who thinks one copy of a recessive allele is expressed makes both recessive. A recessive allele is only expressed if two copies are present.

options.text: Polydactyly recessive; cystic fibrosis is dominant
options.rationale: A student who assumes the more serious disorder must come from a dominant allele swaps the two. Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele and cystic fibrosis by a recessive allele.

mcqs.stem: A couple are offered embryo screening. Which of these is an ethical issue they might consider?

options.text: Whether one gene controls all the embryo's traits
options.rationale: A student who thinks one gene controls each characteristic raises a genetics point, not an ethical one. Most characteristics result from multiple genes interacting.

options.text: Whether the screening test is medically accurate
options.rationale: A student who sees screening only as a medical procedure judges it by accuracy. The issues to weigh are economic, social and ethical.

options.text: Whether rejecting an embryo with an allele is right
options.rationale: Embryo screening raises economic, social and ethical issues, and whether it is right to reject an embryo because of the alleles it carries is an ethical judgement.

options.text: Whether a gene codes for a trait or for a protein
options.rationale: A student focused on how genes work raises a factual question. A gene codes for a sequence of amino acids to make a protein, and this is not an ethical issue.

mcqs.stem: What do ordinary human body cells contain?

options.text: 23 pairs of chromosomes, one pair determining sex
options.rationale: Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex.

options.text: 23 chromosomes in total, one of them determining sex
options.rationale: A student who drops the word 'pairs' halves the number. Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes.

options.text: 23 pairs of chromosomes, with XY in every female
options.rationale: A student who swaps the labels puts XY in females. In females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX); in males they are different (XY).

options.text: 23 pairs of chromosomes, all from the mother's egg
options.rationale: A student who credits the mother with all the genetic material picks this. Gametes join at fertilisation, each carrying a single set of chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: A genetic cross is carried out between XX and XY parents. What does it predict about the offspring?

options.text: 1 female to 1 male, so a 50% chance of each
options.rationale: The cross gives XX, XX, XY and XY, a simple ratio of 1 female to 1 male, so there is a 50% probability of each sex.

options.text: Exactly 2 girls and 2 boys in four babies
options.rationale: A student who reads the four boxes as four actual children states a certainty. The cross predicts probability, so the children actually born may differ.

options.text: All female, as the egg cell decides sex
options.rationale: A student who thinks the mother determines sex expects only her X chromosomes to count. The XY parent's gamete carries either an X or a Y.

options.text: 3 females to 1 male, as X is dominant here
options.rationale: A student who treats X as a dominant allele applies the 3 to 1 ratio. The sex chromosomes are XX in females and XY in males, giving a 1 to 1 ratio.
